prompt: What does CAP theorem actually say, and why is partition tolerance basically mandatory?
answer_markdown: CAP theorem states that during a network partition, a distributed system can guarantee either full consistency or full availability, but not both. Partition tolerance is treated as mandatory because in any real system with multiple machines connected over a network, some link will eventually fail or lag — you can't opt out of the possibility, so the real design decision is what happens when it occurs, not whether to plan for it.

prompt: Design a ticket-booking system for a popular concert. Would you lean CP or AP, and why?
answer_markdown: You'd lean CP for the actual seat-reservation step, because overselling the same seat to two people is a worse outcome than briefly refusing a booking request — correctness matters more than uptime for that specific operation. However, you could still make the browsing/search experience AP, showing possibly-stale seat availability while people browse, and only enforcing strict consistency at the final confirm-and-pay step. This tests whether you know CAP trade-offs can be applied per-operation rather than as one blanket decision for the whole system.

prompt: How does PACELC extend CAP theorem, and why was it introduced?
answer_markdown: PACELC points out that CAP only describes behavior during a Partition (P), forcing a choice between Availability and Consistency (the 'AC' half) — but even when there's no partition at all, a system still has to choose between Latency and Consistency (the 'ELC' half), because waiting to fully synchronize replicas takes time. It was introduced because CAP alone doesn't explain everyday trade-offs in normal operation, only outage behavior. Interviewers who bring this up are checking whether you know CAP's real-world limitations, not just the textbook triangle.

prompt: Can a system be CA (consistent and available) in practice?
answer_markdown: Only if it never has to deal with a network partition, which realistically only holds for a single-node system with no network between replicas. The moment you have more than one node communicating over a network, partitions become possible, so CA isn't a practical option for any genuinely distributed system — you have to plan for what happens when the network fails.
